Linear Regression Part II

  • How do we test hypotheses related to coefficients?

  • How do we assess model “fit”?

  • How do we control for additional characteristics?

Linear Regression model

  • My dependent variable is % voter turnout in a state

  • My independent variable is the partisan lean in that state. (lower values indicate a state is more evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats)

  • What is the effect of a one unit increase on voter turnout?

  • What is the % turnout in a state where partisan lean is zero?

term estimate
(Intercept) 65.1
partisan_lean -0.4

Uncertainty in coefficients

How much should we trust our estimates here?

Uncertainty in coefficients

  • \(\hat{\beta_1}\) (the estimated coefficient) is an estimate just like a sample mean. So it can be “off” the true value due to random chance.

  • The “null hypothesis” in this scenario is that the actual slope of this line is 0.

  • In this case: can we rule out the possibility that random error would give us a coefficient absolutely greater than what we see in our sample? And can we identify a range that we’re fairly certain contains the correct value for \(\beta_1\)?

term estimate
(Intercept) 65.1
partisan_lean -0.4

Uncertainty in coefficients

Lucky for us: the central limit theorem applies to regression coefficients! We just need to get an estimate of the standard error of \(\beta_1\)

Uncertainty in coefficients: sources of error

We to get the standard error for the regression coefficient.

Beyond the sample size, we need to think about two additional sources of error for \(\hat{\beta_1}\)

Uncertainty in coefficients: sources of error

First: more variability around the regression line means more uncertainty around our coefficient estimates.

  • Intuitively: if there’s a lot of “noise” around Y, then its harder to estimate things precisely.

Uncertainty in coefficients: sources of error

Second: More variability in the independent variable means less uncertainty.

  • Less intuitive!

  • but errors have more influence when X has less variability

Standard error of a slope

\(S_{yx}\) represents the “standard error of the regression”. Note that the numerator here is the same as the error sum of squares.

\[ S_{yx} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum{(\hat{y_i} - y_i)^2}}{n-2}} \]

The denominator here accounts for the amount of variation in X. Note that more variability in X means that we will have a smaller standard error.

\[ SE(\beta_1) = \frac{s_{yx}}{\sqrt{\sum^n_{i=1}{(X_i -\bar{X})^2}}} \]

Standard error of the intercept

We can also calculate the standard error for the intercept, but generally speaking we don’t care because we rarely test hypotheses about the intercept.

\[ SE(\hat{\beta}_0) = s_{yx} \times \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}+\frac{\bar{X}^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})^2}} \]

Standard error of a slope

Back to our model…

Confidence Interval for a slope

From here, things aren’t that different from what we already know.

Get a rough estimate of the 95% confidence interval for the coefficient by doubling the standard error and then adding and subtracting it from the estimate.

term estimate std.error lower 95% CI upper 95% CI
(Intercept) 65.08 1.60 61.88 68.29
partisan_lean -0.37 0.17 -0.72 -0.03

P.value for a slope

Or calculate a t-statistic by dividing the estimate by its standard error, then find the associated p-value:

term estimate std.error statistic p.value
(Intercept) 65.08 1.60 40.65 0.00
partisan_lean -0.37 0.17 -2.15 0.04

Statistical Significance for a slope

Can we reject the null hypothesis that the coefficient for partisan_lean is actually 0?

term estimate std.error statistic p.value lower 95% CI upper 95% CI
(Intercept) 65.08 1.60 40.65 0.00 61.88 68.29
partisan_lean -0.37 0.17 -2.15 0.04 -0.72 -0.03

Regression output in R

  • IV absolute value of the Cook Partisan Voting Index in a state in 2020

  • DV % voter turnout in a state

states$absolute_cook_index <- abs(states$cook.index)
regC(vep20.turnout ~ absolute_cook_index, data=states)

Model fit

How did Maryland do relative to expectations in 2020? Are we over performing or under performing on turnout? In general, how well does the model “fit” the data?

R-squared: model fit

We often want to talk about how well a model “fits” the data. \(R^2\) is one way to evaluate this.

  • \(R^2\) value is the proportion of variance in Y explained by variance in our independent variables.

  • \(R^2\) will always range from 0 to 1. Its a proportion. A score of 1 would mean that our model perfectly predicts Y.

  • You can think of \(R^2\) as a measure of how well the model predicts outcomes.

R-squared

  • Calculating the error sum of squares was part of fitting the regression line
  • The total sum of squares is just a measure of all the variance in Y.
  • So, taking \(\frac{TSS-ESS}{TSS}\) should give us a measure of the variance explained relative to the total variance.
  • About 19% of the variation in voter turnout is explained by variation in the independent variable.

R-squared

  • Note that our output also includes “Adjusted R-squared”

  • Adjusted R-squared accounts for a tendency of normal R-squared stats to increase even when we include bad predictors in our model.

  • The two values will usually remain close, and the interpretation is more-or-less the same.

regC(vep20.turnout ~ absolute_cook_index, data=states)

R-squared values

  • Keep in mind: \(R^2\) can be high even if X has a weak effect and low when X has a strong effect. It depends, in part, on how much variability there is in the dependent variable.

Multiple Regression: how do we account for other stuff?

Checking for confounders

  • On closer examination, I notice that a lot of states with fewer college grads are in the low turnout group.

  • So is it possible that education is a confounding variable here?

Checking for confounders

Running a second regression model suggests there’s some kind of relationship here.

term estimate std.error statistic
(Intercept) 44.0 3.9 11.2
ba.or.more 0.7 0.1 6.2

Multiple Regression

  • In the past, we handled this by splitting up the data into groups, but - we would lose a lot of statistical power if we split up the data like this.

  • Instead, we’re going to account for this potential confounding variable by mathematically “holding constant” for the other variables in the model.

Multiple Regression

Remember that this was the formula for a prediction of Y

\[ \hat{y} = \alpha + \beta_1x \]

When we consider the actual values of Y, we’ve got this error term that represents the distance between the prediction and the observation:

\[ y_i = \alpha + \beta_1x + \epsilon \]

Multiple Regression

In a sense, a regression model splits the data up into two categories:

\[ y_i = \alpha + \beta_1x_i + \epsilon_i \]

  • \(\alpha + \beta_1x\) represents the part of Y that we can explain with our model.

  • \(\epsilon\) represents the part of Y that is not explained by our model.

Multiple Regression

So what do I get if I subtract \(\hat{y}\) from each observation in my original model?

state % BA or more Turnout Predicted Turnout Observed - Predicted
AL 26.3 63.1 63.6 -0.5
HI 33.6 57.5 69.0 -11.5
MA 45.0 72.1 77.5 -5.4
NM 27.7 61.3 64.6 -3.3
SD 29.7 66.0 66.1 -0.1

Observed and predicted turnout in select states

Multiple Regression

  • \(Y - \hat{Y}\) would leave me with a measure of turnout that is no longer correlated with education levels.
  • I could do the same thing with the absolute Cook Index by estimating the effect of Education on Cook Index and then taking the residual from that model.
  • Now, if I run my original regression on these residuals, I get an estimate of the effect of absolute Cook Index after removing the effect of education.

Multiple Regression

We don’t need to do all this by hand. Instead, we can add additional controls by just adding a + sign followed by an additional variable:

regC(vep20.turnout ~ absolute_cook_index +  ba.or.more, data=states)

Multiple Regression: interpretation

  • The intercept term now represents the expected value when ALL predictors are equal to zero
  • Each slope represent the effect of a one unit change in that variable controlling for everything else in the model
  • The \(R^2\) statistic represents the amount of variation in Y explained variation in all of the IVs.

Multiple Regression: comparing models
